meta.regime: Two of yesterday's three legs reversed inside a single session. October core CPI at plus 0.3% m/m for a third consecutive month pushed the US 10-year to roughly 4.98% and briefly above 5%, took a December hike to effectively fully priced with a live half-point tail, and the dollar index closed at 102.303 having gained on all seven other majors on the week. At the same time the Iran de-escalation trade stalled - Tehran's security chief says no negotiations are under way and Washington says the blockade stands - so the crude collapse that was dismantling the Canadian and Australian hawkish cases has paused, with WTI back at 86.616 and Brent at 92.508. The board is no longer four firming currencies against two broken commodity ones; it is one dollar that is being paid for its rate case against seven that are not.

dailyRead: Yesterday this file argued that the dollar had stopped being paid for its rate case and came down to plus one, and it named the condition for reversing that: a rally on a firm core. The core printed at plus 0.3% m/m against a plus 0.2% forecast, the third consecutive month at that pace, headline at plus 0.4% against plus 0.3%, and the dollar did exactly what it had refused to do for a week. The index is 102.303 and plus 0.73% on the week, and it gained on every one of the seven other majors - EUR/USD minus 0.63%, GBP/USD minus 0.97%, AUD/USD minus 1.86%, NZD/USD minus 0.28%, USD/JPY plus 0.23%, USD/CHF plus 1.12%, USD/CAD plus 1.64%. The transmission was through the long end: the 10-year went to about 4.98% and briefly through 5%, the two-year toward 4.75%, and that is the single most important number on the board today because it reprices every haven and every carry trade at once. The pricing detail matters and yesterday's note needs correcting. A December hike is now effectively fully owned; what is live is the size. CME FedWatch has the 25bp bucket near 85% and the 50bp bucket at roughly 11% to 15%, up from about 1% before the print, because Governor Waller had said hours earlier that a half-point should be considered if October core came in around 0.3% or higher, and it did. So the marginal dollar buyer from here is paying for a half-point, not for a hike, which is a much narrower edge than the headline odds suggest. The dollar goes back to plus two and strengthening, and EUR/USD and GBP/USD return to shorts. The second thing that changed is the one that rescues the commodity bloc from yesterday's framing. The de-escalation trade has stalled on the record: Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei says no negotiations are currently under way, the foreign minister blames the US midterms, Trump says the Gulf states would prefer the status quo of a continued naval blockade, and attacks on tankers near the Strait have not stopped. Brent fell below 90 dollars for the first time since August on Tuesday and then bounced - it is 92.508 and plus 1.11% today, with WTI 86.616 and plus 0.67%, both off two-month lows. That does not restore the October premium, but it does stop the one-way bleed that was the whole bear case for the loonie and the Aussie, and it is why the ranking at the bottom of the board changes today. Canada improves from minus two to minus one, and the specific facts are these: the Summary of Deliberations published Tuesday evening came out harder than this file expected. The Governing Council agreed there could be a need to increase the policy rate further, said it would take decisions one meeting at a time, documented that oil was about 35 dollars a barrel above the July Report assumption, kept CPI at 3.5% for year-end and above 3% for much of 2027, and noted that higher costs have largely not been passed to consumers yet while business surveys point to price rises over the coming year. That last point is the one that matters most, because it means the inflation impulse is still ahead of the data rather than behind it. The bear case survives - unemployment at a six-month-high 6.7%, employment minus 4,700 after minus 68,300, core at 2.2% which is the softest on this board outside Japan and Switzerland, and a loonie that lost to all seven other majors - but it is no longer the clean sweep it was, so USD/CAD stays a long and CAD/JPY stays a short at medium rather than high conviction. Australia takes the bottom instead and moves to minus two. It was the worst major on the week at minus 1.86% and it lost to all seven, and the reason is structural rather than a single print: the November 3 hike to 4.85% passed on a 6-3 vote with three members preferring a hold, which is the clearest signal available that 4.85% is the peak and December 8 is a pause. Copper will not help - 6.3048, minus 1.53% on the week and minus 5.88% on the month - and September employment fell 39,329. The domestic residue is still genuine at a 4.3% CPI with core 3.6%, the highest inflation on this board, and that is why this is minus two rather than minus three; the November 17 minutes at 02:30 are the only test before the meeting. Sterling is the day's genuine discovery and it runs against what this file wrote yesterday. The claim was that Bailey had walked away from December. The verified pricing says otherwise: a December 17 hike is now around 70%, from about 50% immediately after the November 5 decision and 30% before it, and one Bloomberg-sourced survey has the UK base rate seen reaching 5%. The decision itself was 8-1 to 4.00% with Catherine Mann dissenting for 4.25%, and Dhingra and Taylor - both previous holds - switched to hiking. Bailey cited a material further increase in energy prices, the Monetary Policy Report has CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year from 3.5%, and his guidance was that the rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved. With the conflict visibly not resolving this week, that condition now points the hawkish way rather than the dovish way. So the ratePath for sterling flips from hold to hike and GBP stays plus one, but the price has not paid for any of it - minus 0.97% to the dollar, minus 0.34% to the euro on the week - which is why GBP/USD is a short at low-medium rather than medium conviction and Thursday's GDP at 09:00 is the reconciliation. The yen also needs a correction, and it is a tradeable one. Yesterday this file called 158.04 the level Tokyo said it would defend. The pair is now 158.807, it went through 158 without an operation, and current reporting puts the intervention risk zone nearer 160 with the authorities warning about disorderly moves rather than defending a specific figure. So 158 was not a line, and the honest read is that the official constraint sits roughly 1.2 yen above spot. The Bank's own case is unchanged and hawkish - the October Summary of Opinions has many members judging a near-term hike necessary and one putting neutral considerably above 1%, with December 17-18 eyed at 1.50% - and the yen gained on six of seven majors again this week, losing only to the dollar. JPY stays plus one, the basket stays a long, and USD/JPY stays a range, but now because the reward to the ceiling is small rather than because the ceiling is here. The euro is the quiet one and that is the point: nothing changed and nothing needed to. December 17 is near-settled at 2.75%, Nagel has called the case strong and Lane called a hike prudent indeed, and the euro sat mid-pack, losing 0.63% to the dollar while beating the franc, the loonie, the Aussie and sterling. It stays plus one, and EUR/AUD at high conviction is the cleanest long on the board. The franc is the cleanest loser of the yield move: it lost 1.12% to the dollar, beat only the Aussie and the loonie, and its only possible leg is a haven bid that a 5% US 10-year actively suppresses. At zero with nothing to decide on December 10 and an October CPI of 1.5% that is roughly 96% energy against core at 0.5%, it stays minus one, and the oil bounce is the one thing that would reverse it. New Zealand keeps its zero on the same split as yesterday: second-best price on the week at minus 0.28%, worst fundamentals on the board with unemployment at 5.7% and the highest since 2016, wages at 2.0% against 3.7% inflation, and a Reserve Bank that held at 2.75% on October 28 in a surprise 4-3 vote while saying tighter policy is still likely, with the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement the real test. Metals split exactly along the real-rate line and that is the clearest confirmation of the regime: gold fell about 2.4% as yields approached 5%, sits at 4054.51 and minus 0.14% on the week, and a hawkish Fed into falling energy is the one combination it cannot absorb, so it turns from a levels trade to a short. Silver is 52.920 and plus 1.27% on the week, beating gold on the industrial leg that data-centre and grid demand supplies, and that divergence inside one week is why it keeps a long while gold does not. Equities stayed firm in Europe despite the yield move, and the two indices are still not the same trade: the DAX is 26,564.20 and plus 0.31%, paid by German gas at 84.66 and minus 8.90% on the week, while the Euro Stoxx 50 is 6,380.00 and plus 0.68%, outperforming for a third session because banks are its heaviest sector and a steeper curve plus a near-certain ECB hike pays that weight directly. Today is thin by construction - US and Canadian markets are closed for Veterans and Remembrance Day and France is out for Armistice - so the honest instruction is that this is a day to hold and size, not to initiate in the dollar-bloc crosses.

today.headline: A December hike is priced near 70%, which reverses the dovish path this file carried yesterday
today.read: The correction is specific. Yesterday the ratePath read hold into February 2027, on the argument that Bailey's condition for hiking again was high energy costs returning. The verified pricing is about 70% for a quarter-point to 4.25% on December 17, having gone from roughly 30% before the November 5 decision to about 50% straight after it, with one survey reporting the base rate seen reaching 5%. The guidance was misread rather than the pricing: Bailey said the November rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved, so it is resolution and not the gas price that stops the Bank - and Tehran said this week that no negotiations are under way. The decision was 8-1 to 4.00% with Mann dissenting for 4.25%, and Dhingra and Taylor switched from hold to hike. CPI is forecast near 5% by mid-2027 from 3.5%, with core 2.8% and rising, unemployment 4.7% and employment plus 102,000. What has not happened is payment: minus 0.97% to the dollar on the week and minus 0.34% to the euro. GBP/USD therefore stays a short but drops to low-medium, and Thursday's GDP at 09:00 is the reconciliation.

today.headline: The deliberations kept a further hike on the table, so Canada comes up from minus two to minus one
today.read: Two legs of yesterday's minus two weakened at once. The Summary of Deliberations published Tuesday evening had the Governing Council agreeing there could be a need to increase the policy rate further, deciding one meeting at a time, recording oil about 35 US dollars a barrel above the July Report assumption, and keeping CPI at 3.5% for year-end and above 3% for much of 2027. The line that matters most is that higher costs have largely not reached consumers yet while business surveys point to price rises over the coming year, which puts the impulse ahead of the data rather than behind it. The second leg is that crude stopped falling - WTI 86.616 and plus 0.67%, Brent 92.508 and plus 1.11% off two-month lows - because the de-escalation trade stalled. What survives is real: unemployment at a six-month-high 6.7%, employment minus 4,700 after minus 68,300, core at 2.2%, and a loonie that lost to all seven others at minus 1.64%. USD/CAD stays the long and CAD/JPY the short, both downgraded to medium. Canada is closed today.

today.headline: Worst major of the week at minus 1.86% and it takes the bottom of the board at minus two
today.read: It lost to all seven other majors, and the reason is a vote rather than a print. The November 3 hike to 4.85% passed 6-3, with three of nine members preferring to leave the cash rate at 4.60%, which is the strongest available signal that 4.85% is the peak and that December 8 is a pause; reporting since has read the split the same way. Of the statement's three justifications, fuel was named first and crude is minus 7.60% on the month despite this week's bounce, while the AI-related technology demand leg is what copper refuses to confirm at 6.3048, minus 1.53% on the week and minus 5.88% on the month. September employment fell 39,329 and unemployment is 4.7%. What keeps this off minus three is that the inflation residue is domestic and the highest on this board - CPI 4.3% with core 3.6% - and it cannot be tested until the minutes on November 17 at 02:30. AUD/USD is the cleanest short on the board, with EUR/AUD and GBP/AUD the cleanest longs.

today.read: The yen lost only to the dollar this week: EUR/JPY minus 0.40%, GBP/JPY minus 0.74%, AUD/JPY minus 1.65%, CAD/JPY minus 1.39%, CHF/JPY minus 0.89%, NZD/JPY minus 0.07%, against USD/JPY plus 0.23%. today.headline: The cleanest loser of the yield move: a 5% US 10-year suppresses the only leg the franc has
today.read: It lost 1.12% to the dollar on the week and beat only the Aussie and the loonie, with EUR/CHF at 0.92208 from about 0.9148 a week ago and CHF/JPY minus 0.89%. The mechanism is the point rather than the move: at a zero policy rate the franc's only possible bid is safe-haven demand, and a 10-year near 4.98% raises the opportunity cost of holding a zero-yielding currency directly. The Bank's own September record says there had been little safe-haven demand since June and that widened differentials had made the franc attractive as a funding currency in carry trades. October CPI of 1.5% is not a case: core is 0.5% and the rise was overwhelmingly energy, so a deflating gas complex unwinds it, and wage growth has slowed to 0.4%. Nothing to decide on December 10, with a Reuters poll having 21 of 25 economists on hold through year-end. Score stays minus one. The live reversal is a Hormuz re-escalation, and this week's stalled talks are a reminder that it has not gone away.

today.headline: Quiet and mid-pack, which is exactly what a near-settled December hike should look like
today.read: The euro lost 0.63% to the dollar on the week while beating the franc at plus 0.49%, the loonie at plus 1.00%, the Aussie at plus 1.25% and sterling at plus 0.34%, and losing to the Kiwi and the yen. Nothing in the policy picture needed to change: a 25bp move to a 2.75% deposit rate on December 17 is effectively priced, Nagel has called the case strong and Lane called a hike prudent indeed, and Goldman expects that single hike while doubting any path significantly above 3%. The evidence underneath is unchanged and still poor - October HICP 4.0% delivered by energy with core flat at 2.5%, wages decelerating to 3.0%, negotiated wages 2.44%, growth 0.4% q/q, unemployment 6.5% - so this stays a terminal hike into a deflating base rather than the start of anything. Score holds at plus one, and the clean expressions remain EUR/AUD, EUR/CAD and EUR/CHF rather than EUR/USD. Lagarde speaks today at 11:45 and Thursday at 21:30; pushback is the risk.

today.headline: Second-best price on the week and the worst fundamentals on the board, so the zero holds
today.read: The Kiwi lost just 0.28% to the dollar and beat the euro, sterling, the franc, the loonie and the Aussie - NZD/CAD plus 1.34% and NZD/AUD plus 1.28% were among the week's firmest crosses. The fundamentals have not moved to meet it: unemployment 5.7% and the highest since 2016, private wage growth 2.0% against 3.7% headline inflation so real wages are negative, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter, growth 0.2% q/q, core 3.2%. The October 28 decision held at 2.75% in a 4-3 vote when about 90% of a hike was priced, with the statement saying tighter policy is still likely, and the December 9 Monetary Policy Statement is where that guidance is finally tested with fresh forecasts. Correction to carry: the next Reserve Bank decision is December 9, and the November 25 date in some coverage is Australia's October monthly CPI. Score stays zero - firm price, weak policy case - which is why EUR/NZD and GBP/NZD stay low-medium longs rather than clean ones.

USD.when: December 9, with new projections and the size - 25 or 50 - the only open question
USD.note: TradingEconomics carries 4.00% for October as the upper bound of the 3.75%-4.00% target range, held on October 28 with two policymakers voting for a hike. October core CPI printed plus 0.3% m/m against a plus 0.2% forecast, the third consecutive month at that pace, with headline plus 0.4% against plus 0.3%; the Bureau of Labor Statistics published no 12-month headline rate because October 2025 data were never collected during the appropriations lapse, so the monthly run-rate is all there is. This settles the hike and reopens the size. Governor Waller said in London hours before the release that he backs 25bp but that a half-point should be considered if October core came in around 0.3% or higher, that hiking only 25bp would put credibility at risk, and that elevated energy prices could affect core inflation well into 2027. CME FedWatch now has the 25bp bucket near 85% and the 50bp bucket at roughly 11% to 15%, up from about 1% before the print, so a hike of some size is effectively fully owned. Yesterday's file reported 25bp at 95% to 99%, which conflated the total hike probability with the quarter-point bucket; the corrected reading is that the quarter-point is the base case and the half-point is the live tail. The supporting data is hawkish on every line: October payrolls plus 165,000 against forecasts near 60,000 with August revised to 186,000, unemployment 4.1%, Q3 growth 3.4%, core 2.6% y/y for September. The 10-year at roughly 4.98% and briefly above 5% is the transmission channel. Friday's PPI at 15:30 is forecast to decelerate to plus 0.4% headline and plus 0.3% core and is the last scheduled data that can soften it. Federal funding runs out December 11, two days after the vote, with Congress in a lame-duck session after the Democrats took both chambers.

EUR.when: December 17, the final 2026 meeting, effectively priced
EUR.note: Deposit facility rate 2.50%, TradingEconomics-verified today from the Deposit Facility Rate row, with the main refinancing rate at 2.65% and the lending rate 2.90%; held on October 29. The December move is now the closest thing to settled on this board. Markets price 25bp to a 2.75% deposit rate at the final meeting of the year, Bundesbank President Nagel has called the case for December strong, Chief Economist Lane said a hike would be prudent indeed if the data stay unchanged, and an October Reuters poll had 64 of 73 economists expecting the move. Goldman Sachs forecasts the same single hike to 2.75% while doubting the market's earlier pricing of a path significantly above 3%, which is the useful qualifier: this is a terminal hike, not the start of a cycle. The evidence underneath still does not improve. The October HICP of 4.0% was delivered by energy with core flat at 2.5% and monthly core at 0.2%, headline wage growth has decelerated to 3.0% and negotiated wages to 2.44%, growth is 0.4% q/q and 1.3% y/y, and unemployment has edged up to 6.5%. Euro-area gas is 85.97 and minus 2.40% on the week with German gas 84.66 and minus 8.90%, so the base the hike is being delivered into keeps deflating - a 2027 policy-error risk, not a December one. Lagarde speaks today at 11:45 and again Thursday at 21:30, and pushback is the main risk to the euro longs; Eurostat finalises October on November 18.

GBP.when: December 17, now priced near 70% - changed from hold in yesterday's file
GBP.note: Bank Rate was raised 25bp to 4.00% on November 5 on an 8-1 vote, with Catherine Mann dissenting in favour of 0.5 points to 4.25%, so every member wanted at least a hike; TradingEconomics carries 4.00% for November against 3.75% previously, the first increase since 2023. Swati Dhingra and Alan Taylor, both of whom had previously favoured holding, voted to increase. This field is corrected today and it is the day's biggest single revision. Yesterday this file read next as hold with February 2027 the next realistic move, on the argument that Bailey's condition for a further hike was high energy costs returning and they were falling instead. The verified pricing contradicts it: swap markets implied about 30% for a December hike before the decision, roughly 50% immediately after it, and the most recent reading is around 70% for a quarter-point to 4.25% on December 17, with one survey reporting the base rate seen reaching 5%. The reason the dovish read was wrong is the wording of the guidance. Bailey cited a material further increase in energy prices as the justification for hiking, and said the rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved - so it is resolution, not the level of gas, that would stop the Bank, and the conflict has visibly stopped resolving this week with Tehran saying no negotiations are under way. The Monetary Policy Report has CPI rising to around 5% by the middle of next year from 3.5% now. The domestic anchor is intact: CPI 3.5% with core 2.8% and both rising, unemployment down to 4.7% from 4.9%, employment plus 102,000, wage growth 3.7%, growth 1.4% y/y. Against all of it the pound has not been paid - minus 0.97% to the dollar and minus 0.34% to the euro on the week. Thursday's GDP m/m at 09:00 is forecast at 0.0% with prelim Q3 at plus 0.7%, and the first CPI print after the decision is November 18.

JPY.when: December 17-18, eight days after the Fed, with 1.50% the expected outcome
JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 in an 8-1 vote, Takata dissenting for a faster move toward neutral; TradingEconomics carries 1.25% for October. The October Summary of Opinions, published Tuesday, points to a good chance of a December move. Many board members judged a near-term rate hike necessary, some argued the Bank should speed up the pace, one said it should move without becoming overly cautious, one put the neutral rate considerably above 1%, and the board judged underlying inflation generally consistent with the 2% target. The counterweight is on the record: some members favoured holding in October to examine risks and the cumulative effect of past hikes, and one warned that with the policy rate already inside the estimated neutral range a further hike could weigh on the economy, with consumption and next year's wage talks flagged as the checks on pace. Governor Ueda has said another hike in December is possible, and market attention is on 1.50% at the December 17-18 meeting. The data supports it: underlying and core inflation both 2.1%, September wage growth accelerating to 4.6% from 3.9%, unemployment 2.4%, growth 0.7% y/y. One correction from yesterday on the constraint above. This file described 158.04 as the level Tokyo said it would defend; the pair has since traded through it to 158.807 with no operation. Current reporting puts the risk zone nearer 160, with the Ministry of Finance reiterating readiness to act against disorderly and excessive yen depreciation and affirming the joint US-Japan currency statement, rather than defending a specific figure. Quarterly data confirmed interventions on three days between July 30 and August 3, the largest 7.98 trillion yen on July 30, and each operation has historically knocked the pair back five yen or more. So the official ceiling is roughly 1.2 yen above spot, not at it. The Fed votes December 9 against the Bank's December 17-18, so a Fed-only move widens the differential for eight days.

AUD.when: December 8, with the November 17 minutes at 02:30 the only test
AUD.note: Hiked 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 on a 6-3 majority - six members for 25bp, three preferring to leave it unchanged at 4.60% - the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008, TradingEconomics-verified for November. The split is the whole story and it is why Australia takes the bottom of the board today rather than Canada. A three-vote dissent at the moment of a hike is the strongest available signal that 4.85% is the peak, and reporting since has read the divided vote as strengthening expectations that the rate stays there. The statement named three reasons: elevated fuel and commodity prices amid the Middle East conflict, tighter domestic capacity constraints, and AI-related demand for technology goods. Fuel was named first and crude is minus 7.60% on the month even after this week's bounce. The AI leg is the one copper will not confirm at 6.3048, minus 1.53% on the week and minus 5.88% on the month. That leaves domestic capacity, which cannot be tested until the minutes are published on November 17 at 02:30. The hawkish residue is real and it is the reason this is minus two rather than minus three: Q3 CPI 4.3% with core 3.6% - the highest inflation on this board - quarterly inflation at 0.8% m/m for September, and a trimmed mean that printed above forecast. Against it, September employment fell 39,329, unemployment has risen to 4.7%, growth has slowed to 2.1% y/y and wage growth is 3.2%. catalysts.event: Bank of Canada Summary of Governing Council Deliberations
catalysts.note: Harder than this file expected, and the reason Canada improves from minus two to minus one today. The Council agreed there could be a need to increase the policy rate further and said it would take decisions one meeting at a time. It recorded that the benchmark oil price was approximately 35 US dollars a barrel higher than assumed in the July Report, kept inflation reaching 3.5% at the end of this year and remaining above 3% for much of 2027, and noted that higher costs have largely not been passed through to consumers so far while business surveys suggest firms expect to raise some prices over the next year. That last line is the genuinely hawkish one: it places the inflation impulse ahead of the data rather than behind it, which is the opposite of a purely imported case about to evaporate. The next decision is December 9.

geopolitics: The de-escalation trade stalled this week, and that single fact reorders the bottom of the board. Start with the record rather than the price. Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei says no negotiations are currently under way between Tehran and Washington, and the foreign minister attributes the stall to the US midterm elections. Tehran continues to insist on its preconditions for reopening the Strait - an end to the war on all fronts, the unfreezing of assets abroad, the lifting of oil sanctions and an end to the naval blockade of Iranian ports - while Washington insists nuclear issues feature in any initial negotiation. Trump has said the Gulf states, naming Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Bahrain and Kuwait, would prefer the status quo of a continued blockade, and a US official describes the blockade as in full force and effect. Attacks on civilian tankers near the Strait of Hormuz have continued. Qatar has carried an Iranian proposal to the White House and is mediating, so the diplomatic channel is open, but open is not the same as progressing. The price has responded accordingly. Brent fell below 90 dollars on Tuesday for the first time since August on Trump's comment that the war could end fairly soon, then rebounded as the talks stalled: Brent is 92.508 and plus 1.11% on the day, WTI 86.616 and plus 0.67%, both off two-month lows, with the month still minus 13.26% and minus 7.60% respectively. The gas complex has stabilised too - euro-area gas 85.97 and minus 2.40% on the week, UK gas 212.95 and minus 2.50%, German gas 84.66 and minus 8.90%, which is still the steepest fall in the complex and the cleanest European signal. The FX read follows from one distinction: the physical war has not ended and the Strait is still effectively closed, so what moved over the past fortnight was the expectation, and this week the expectation stopped moving. First, that changes the oil position from a short to a range rather than reversing it. Roughly a fifth of the barrel's value has already come out this month, so the premium available to drain has largely drained, and from 86 dollars a re-escalation is the larger tail - which is why USOIL goes to range at low-medium with levels at 84.00 to 90.00. Second, it rescues Canada from the bottom of the board, and the deliberations did the rest: the Governing Council agreed there could be a need to increase the policy rate further and noted that higher costs have largely not reached consumers yet, so the Canadian inflation impulse is prospective rather than spent. Canada moves to minus one and Australia takes the bottom at minus two, on a 6-3 vote that caps the cash rate and a copper price that will not confirm the AI-demand leg. Third, it keeps the franc short honest rather than comfortable. The franc is minus 1.12% on the week because a US 10-year near 4.98% suppresses the haven bid mechanically, and the SNB's own September record says there had been little safe-haven demand since June - but a Hormuz re-escalation is precisely the event that would re-bid it faster than yields can suppress it, so CHF/JPY remains both the cleanest expression and the named test. Fourth, it changes what the Bank of England's guidance means. Bailey justified the November hike on a material further increase in energy prices and said the rise was unlikely to be the last unless the conflict is resolved, so the trigger for stopping is resolution and not the gas price - and with resolution stalling, December pricing has gone to about 70%. That is the correction to yesterday's dovish sterling path. Fifth, the dollar needs none of this: its case is domestic, it votes on December 9 and the CPI that settled the question covered October. It is the only currency on the board whose path does not depend on what happens in the Gulf, and this week it was also the only one being paid. Sixth, the equity read stays split by sector rather than geography. German gas at minus 8.90% on the week pays the DAX's industrial weight, while the Euro Stoxx 50's heavier bank weight is paid by a near-certain ECB hike and a steepening global curve, which is why EU50 has now outperformed GER40 for three sessions and why the two indices carry different conviction.
